overview: Sibylla of Jerusalem was queen during the crisis that led to Hattin and the loss of Jerusalem. Her marriage to Guy of Lusignan placed dynastic legitimacy and factional politics on a collision course.
Her legacy is often overshadowed by male commanders, but the crisis of Jerusalem cannot be understood without her dynastic authority.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sibylla of Jerusalem was queen during the crisis that led to Hattin and the loss of Jerusalem. Her marriage to Guy of Lusignan placed dynastic legitimacy and factional politics on a collision course.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Sibylla was daughter of Amalric I and sister of Baldwin IV, making her central to the succession once Baldwin’s illness became unavoidable.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Sibylla of Jerusalem is remembered for the fierce loyalty to her husband that placed Guy of Lusignan on the throne against the wishes of much of the nobility, and her character survives chiefly through that act of determined devotion. The sources present a queen who held the hereditary right to the crown and who, when pressed to set aside the unpopular Guy, is said to have agreed to be crowned alone — and then defiantly crowned her husband with her own hands.

That episode, whether recorded with admiration or dismay, fixed her reputation for stubborn personal attachment over political calculation, a choice that her critics blamed for the disasters that followed. The chroniclers, writing in the shadow of Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem, tended to judge her loyalty as a costly weakness.

What the record allows is the picture of a queen who valued her marriage above the counsel of her barons and who used her hereditary claim decisively, if controversially. She is remembered for that singular act of devotion — the crowning of Guy — which secured her husband's kingship and, in the eyes of the tradition, helped seal the kingdom's fate. Her own inner character beyond this remains lightly documented.

contentSections.title: As queen of Jerusalem
paragraphs: Sibylla defended Guy’s claim despite opposition from leading nobles. Her choice preserved marital loyalty and dynastic continuity but intensified political divisions at the worst possible moment.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Sibylla died of disease during the siege of Acre in 1190, along with her daughters, weakening Guy’s claim to the kingdom.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Her legacy is often overshadowed by male commanders, but the crisis of Jerusalem cannot be understood without her dynastic authority.
